question.problem:
Using the normal approximation to the binomial distribution, approximate the probability of getting $30$ odd numbers on $70$ rolls of a $6$-sided die. Give your final answer to three decimal places. *Hint: The data below is taken from the table of values of the cumulative distribution function $Φ(z)$ for the standard normal distribution. *
$z$$\,0.00\,$$\,0.01\,$$\,0.02\,$
$\,-1.3\,$ $\,0.0968\,$ $\,0.0951\,$ $\,0.0934\,$
$\,-1.2\,$ $\,0.1151\,$ $\,0.1131\,$ $\,0.1112\,$
$\,-1.1\,$ $\,0.1357\,$ $\,0.1335\,$ $\,0.1314\,$
$\,-1.0\,$ $\,0.1587\,$ $\,0.1562\,$ $\,0.1539\,$
$z$$\,0.07\,$$\,0.08\,$$\,0.09\,$
$\,-1.3\,$ $\,0.0854\,$ $\,0.0838\,$ $\,0.0823\,$
$\,-1.2\,$ $\,0.1020\,$ $\,0.1003\,$ $\,0.0985\,$
$\,-1.1\,$ $\,0.1210\,$ $\,0.1190\,$ $\,0.1170\,$
$\,-1.0\,$ $\,0.1423\,$ $\,0.1401\,$ $\,0.1379\,$
question.worked_solution:
Given a binomial random variable $X∼B(n,p),$ if 

- $np>5,$ and

- $n(1-p)>5,$

we can approximate $X$ as a normal random variable $Y$ with mean $\mu =np$ and variance ${\sigma }^{2}=np(1-p),$ that is, 

$$
Y∼N(np,np(1-p)).
$$

Here, we have $n=70$ and $p=0.5.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}np & =70\cdot 0.5 \\  & =35 \\  & >5\,✓ \\ n(1-p) & =70\cdot (1-0.5) \\  & =35 \\  & >5.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can approximate our binomial random variable $X$ with a normal random variable $Y$ with mean

$$
\mu =np=(70)(0.5)=35
$$

and variance

$$
{\sigma }^{2}=np(1-p)=(70)(0.5)(1-0.5)=17.5.
$$

That is, we can approximate $X$ by $Y∼N(35,17.5).$

Now, we can approximate the desired probability $P(X=30).$ Using a continuity correction, we have

$$
P(X=30)≈P(29.5\le Y\le 30.5).
$$

To compute this probability, we transform to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(29.5\le Y\le 30.5) & =P(\frac{29.5-35}{\sqrt{17.5}}\le Z\le \frac{30.5-35}{\sqrt{17.5}}) \\  & ≈P(-1.31\le Z\le -1.08) \\  & =P(Z\le -1.08)-P(Z<-1.31) \\  & =P(Z\le -1.08)-P(Z\le -1.31) \\  & =Φ(-1.08)-Φ(-1.31) \\  & =0.1401-0.0951 \\  & =0.045\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
P(X=30)≈0.045.
$$

Note: Using a software package for the approximation gives a probability of $0.0469.$
